The time-resolved gas-analysis results are shown in Figure 9. The blue trace represents hydrogen signal intensity, while the orange trace indicates the background methane concentration. Upon plasma ignition at approximately 1,700 seconds, the hydrogen signal increased sharply; however, the background methane concentration was not significantly affected, reflecting its dominance in the overall gas composition. A subsequent power increase from 14 W to 18 W further elevated the hydrogen signal, confirming the direct correlation between power input and hydrogen yield. The plasma was then switched off, leading to an immediate reduction in hydrogen signal intensity. Figure 9. Time-dependent hydrogen signal intensity and background methane concentration during plasma-on and plasma-off cycles at 14–18 W. Hydrogen signal intensity increases sharply upon plasma ignition and further increases with higher power input, while the methane background remains relatively constant due to its dominance in the gas composition. At higher repetition frequencies between 10 kHz and 100 kHz, the pulse duration was reduced to increase the average power delivery without inducing thermal stress on the electrical switching components. This approach successfully doubled the effective plasma energy density while maintaining stable operation. Quantitative mass spectrometry data collected at 10 kHz and 137 W (Figure 10) revealed a 9.2 percent reduction in methane concentration, an 8 percent increase in hydrogen, and a 52 percent increase in acetylene (C H ) compared to baseline plasma-off 2 2 conditions. These changes confirm that non-thermal plasma reactions effectively decompose methane into hydrogen and reactive hydrocarbons through dissociative excitation and radical- chain mechanisms.
